column1: # The DEVELOPMENT cluster's topics: somebody's laptop.
# One row per topic, tab-separated, in this order:
#   name <TAB> partitions <TAB> replication <TAB> configs
# "replication" is what we would LIKE. Kafka refuses to create a topic whose replication factor is
# higher than the number of brokers it has, and this cluster is a single broker, so seed.sh counts
# the brokers first and lowers any number above that count. Everything here asks for 1 anyway,
# because a laptop has one broker and pretending otherwise would be the wrong picture.
# "configs" is a SEMICOLON-separated list of Kafka topic-level configuration keys, passed straight
# through to `kafka-topics.sh --config`. Use `-` for "no configuration, take the broker defaults".
# Semicolons rather than commas because a Kafka config VALUE can itself contain a comma:
# `cleanup.policy=compact,delete` is one setting, not two.
# WHAT THIS CLUSTER IS FOR. It is the small, scruffy one. Five topics, a couple of partitions
# each, short retention, one leftover test topic nobody cleaned up, and a single consumer group
# that is a little behind. Its job in the demo is to be the thing you switch AWAY from: put it
# beside the production cluster in the cluster switcher and the difference in scale is immediately
# legible, which is the argument for managing several clusters in one place.
# Three of these topics have the same names as topics on the production cluster, on purpose. It is
# the same application deployed twice, which is what a development cluster actually is, and it
# means switching clusters shows you the same topic at two different sizes rather than two
# unrelated lists.
# The application's main stream. Three partitions because that is what somebody types when they
# are not thinking about it, and it is plenty on a laptop.
orders.v1
# 1 day. Nobody keeps a week of test data on their own machine.
# The compacted table of customers. One partition: this is a laptop.
customers.profiles
# Plain text, not JSON. The message browser has to show a value it cannot parse without pretending
# it failed, and this is the topic that proves it does.
audit.log.raw
# 7 days.
# The topic somebody made while debugging on a Tuesday and never deleted. It has no data file, so
# it is created and left EMPTY — which is itself worth having on screen. An empty topic is a real
# state, and a topic list where every row has messages never shows you what zero looks like.
scratch.jm-test
# 1 hour.
# An internal topic. A leading underscore is the convention for "this belongs to a piece of
# infrastructure, not to you", and user interfaces hide these behind a "show internal topics"
# switch. This is where Confluent Schema Registry keeps its schemas, with the configuration it
# insists on.
_schemas
